answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
The GHGP has the opportunity to offer an incredibly valuable framework for voluntary buyers, including by developing a consequential method that is relevant in practice by ensuring feasibility, suitability for target-setting, and consistency with other corporate reporting frameworks.

A consequential method for electricity-sector actions can incentivize companies to act in ways that will reduce carbon emissions systemwide. For example, it can incentivize companies to procure clean energy in locations that achieve the greatest emissions reductions. A consequential method can also help avoid overstating the impact of a company’s actions.

To capitalize on this opportunity, the GHGP needs to ensure the consequential method will be relevant in practice. There are three key aspects to this: engaging with buyers, enabling target-setting, and ensuring consistency with other corporate reporting.

Engagement: We strongly recommend that the GHGP actively includes corporate energy buyers in the development of the method, perhaps adding pilot testing, so that practical issues for corporate reporting are addressed early, and key aspects for decarbonizing the electricity sector — such as the scaling of batteries [1] — are considered.

Target-setting: A key driver for practical relevance for corporate users is whether a framework can be used for setting targets and measuring progress. While target-setting itself is not in the scope of the GHGP, it can play a crucial role in enabling target-setting frameworks to use the consequential method. In its current state, it is not clear if the consequential method will have the necessary elements to make it suitable for target-setting. We strongly recommend that the GHGP should consider including induced emissions, in addition to avoided emissions.

Consistency: As currently proposed, the GHGP does not explain how the method will be integrated with other corporate reporting frameworks. Given the reporting framework elements are to be further developed by the AMI Technical Working Group, and that they have inherent interplay with the Scope 2 Guidance, it is critical that the GHGP does not “lock in” any decisions on Scope 2 reporting requirements before the working group has assessed consistency across the full value chain inventory report.

This goes for both physical deliverability requirements within the definition of the Scope 2 contractual inventory (and whether that aligns with Scopes 1 and 3 contractual inventory), and for the decision to fundamentally alter the contractual, market-based inventory without a clear alternative (i.e., consequential) being fully developed.

Please note that the endorsement of a consequential method should not be used to justify requiring hourly matching and physical deliverability under the Scope 2 market-based method. CEBA opposes mandatory hourly matching and physical deliverability requirements.

[1] See the study below of a battery pilot that a CEBA member company conducted to understand the impacts of various build and operating margin weightings. Since batteries affect both load and generation, reporting only avoided emissions would not adequately capture their emissions impact. Given the critical role batteries can play in grid decarbonization, the GHGP should consider industry research on how GHG accounting rules impact the scaling and emissions impact of this technology. Such studies can inform important methodological questions to make the consequential method both rigorous and practically relevant.

BESS Pilot Case Study (Preprint Version) https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lUubbTZOgBFEZhr1GzwiwAkf5N3Xjx7Z/view

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
While CEBA maintains that the formula is still insufficient for the reasons summarized below, CEBA does so recognizing that the tasked subgroup of the Scope 2 Technical Working Group (TWG) undertook a tremendous amount of work to formulate how to quantify emissions impacts from electricity projects. The Scope 2 TWG experts provided foundational input that should be seriously considered by the AMI TWG.

CEBA answered “no” to question 19 to point out that the formula needs to be tested, ideally in a pilot with respondents potentially interested in adopting the consequential method, to ensure it is not missing key elements that enable target-setting and recognition mechanisms.

For example, companies require a standard and guidance for measuring the induced emissions from consumption-related activities, as well as the avoided emissions from procured generation. By measuring these two components of impact, it becomes possible for target-setting and recognition frameworks to enable target-setting as a means of achieving emissions-reduction targets.

We strongly recommend that the GHGP consider including induced emissions, in addition to avoided emissions. CEBA would like to point out that the statement made by members of the Scope 2 TWG subgroup [1] had put forth a formula that included induced emissions.
[1] marginalimpactmethod.org

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
The current equation needs more consideration for practical use, particularly for target-setting and recognition. It lacks key components needed to evaluate real-world outcomes. In order for the consequential metric to be practically relevant for respondents, the GHGP should consider incorporating induced emissions in addition to avoided emissions. This would make the consequential method suitable for frameworks focused on target-setting and recognition, which is a key criterion for corporate users when considering whether or not to use a framework.

To expand on the above, the GHGP should consider adjusting the current impact metric to reflect both induced and avoided emissions, so it captures the net emissions impact of an entity’s actions on the grid. Without induced emissions, the metric reflects only part of system impacts and can overstate climate benefits.

For example, an entity could procure clean electricity while operating electricity-intensive processes during high-emissions hours and still report a positive impact without accounting for the emissions induced by that carbon-intensive consumption.

This is especially important for grid-interactive technologies such as energy storage, where outcomes depend not only on when electricity is consumed but also when it is delivered back to the grid.

Respondents need clear guidance for quantifying induced emissions from consumption-related activities alongside avoided emissions from procured generation. Measuring both components reduces the risk of overstating impacts and provides a more accurate, decision-relevant picture of what actually changed on the grid as a result of procurement and operational choices.
